title: Madhav Agasti: The Tailor Who Dressed Mogambo and Built Bollywood's Villains
excerpt: In a memoir five decades in the making, master tailor Madhav Agasti reveals how a seven-day, ₹35,000 assignment for Shekhar Kapur's Mr. India produced one of cinema's most enduring villain looks.
body:
• Madhav Agasti, a self-taught Bandra tailor with no formal training, designed Mogambo's costume for Shekhar Kapur's Mr. India (1987) after a brief to fuse a “foreign general” with an Indian zamindar.
  • The look — an all-black coat with golden monogram prints, a long frilled shirt, breeches and long riding boots — was built in seven days for ₹25,000, and producer Boney Kapoor added a ₹10,000 bonus.
  • Across a 50-year career Agasti has dressed more than 350 films, including Andaz Apna Apna, Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, Ghulam and Hera Pheri, alongside political leaders; his memoir Stitching Stardom recounts the journey.
  • Industry figures including Maharashtra's chief minister and stars like Akshay Kumar and Jackie Shroff recently gathered in Mumbai to honour his golden jubilee.

Ask anyone raised on Hindi cinema to finish the sentence “Mogambo…” and they will answer, grinning: “khush hua.” The line arrives with a picture — an all-black coat with gold flourishes, a frilled shirt, breeches, long riding boots, and the epaulettes of a foreign general crossed with an Indian landlord. That image, of Amrish Puri as the tyrant of Shekhar Kapur's Mr. India (1987), was cut, stitched and finished in seven days by a Bombay tailor with no formal training. His name is Madhav Agasti, and five decades into his craft, he has finally told his story in a new memoir.

A seven-day brief, a ₹35,000 costume

Agasti recounts in Stitching Stardom: For Icons, On and Off Screen that director Shekhar Kapur and producer Boney Kapoor walked into his shop with an unusual brief: a villain's costume that blended a foreign dictator with a traditional Indian landlord, according to coverage of the book. With that, Agasti went to work. He dug through foreign newspapers, magazines and books on film history, cutting and pinning references until the look settled: a black coat with golden monogram prints, a long frilled shirt, breeches and tall riding boots of the kind colonial-era zamindars wore, with epaulettes on the shoulders lending the Western military edge, Agasti told The Hollywood Reporter India in a recent interview.

https://x.com/htlifeandstyle/status/2107052198261830012

“I used an all-black coat along with breeches and long riding boots that zamindars in the colonial era would wear. The Western vibe came from the epaulettes on his shoulder straps.”

— Madhav Agasti, costume designer, to The Hollywood Reporter India

Seven days later the costume was done, for a fee of ₹25,000 — with Boney Kapoor so taken by the craftsmanship that he added ₹10,000 more as a reward, bringing Agasti's total to ₹35,000. Amrish Puri's reaction sealed it: the actor grinned at his reflection and declared, “Mogambo… khush hua,” dissolving the line between performer and character before a single scene was shot.

Fifty years behind the cutting table

Agasti began with none of the advantages his reputation now suggests. “I would stand for hours watching senior tailors work, memorising every movement of their fingers. There was no teacher, no apprenticeship,” he said in an interview with t2ONLINE, describing his early years in Mumbai. “My classroom was the street, and my textbook was observation.” From that start, he opened his store, Madhav Agasti, in Bandra in 1975, and went on to dress more than 350 films — Andaz Apna Apna (1994), Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995), Ghulam (1998), Hera Pheri (2000), 36 China Town (2006), plus Agneepath and Aashiqui, per industry coverage. His practice ran deeper than fabric: Agasti also trained as a makeup artist and wig-maker, believing, as he put it, that “the hairline, the wig, the beard, the makeup — these are what give the costume its soul.”

His clientele extended into public life. Coverage of his work notes political clients including Sushil Kumar Shinde, Sharad Pawar and M.M. Joshi, and a recent anniversary profile credits him with the crisp white shirts and saffron drapes that became Balasaheb Thackeray's visual signature. The golden jubilee of his craft was marked at Mumbai's Taj Lands End, where Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, stars Akshay Kumar and Jackie Shroff, Boney Kapoor, Anupam Kher and Gulshan Grover gathered to honour him.

How a costume became a cultural artifact

Mogambo's wardrobe did not merely dress a villain — it argued that costume is character before dialogue. Agasti has described the design's starting point as imagining a man “who believed he ruled the world even when he entered a room alone” — power mixed with madness — and the garment carried that psychology onto the screen, giving the character presence in every frame before Puri spoke a word. The strategy worked so thoroughly that the line escaped the film: Shekhar Kapur has recalled crowds at cricket matches holding placards reading “Mogambo khush hua,” and Amrish Puri joked to the director about fans demanding the line at every function he attended.

“Mumbai trains your eyes before it trains your hands. The city taught me that clothes are not just fabric; they are emotion and identity.”

— Madhav Agasti, in an interview with t2ONLINE

The broader lesson of his career is that Indian costume design has long been auteur work hiding in plain sight. Critics and scholars dissect cinematography and score; the tailor who decided that a villain should look like a cross between a European marshal and a feudal landlord rarely gets a byline. Agasti's 50-year run — and the fact that the fashion press now profiles him for “redefining power dressing for men in India” — suggests that credit is catching up with the craft.

A diaspora icon, stitched by hand

For the Indian diaspora, Mogambo is not nostalgia — he is continuity. Mr. India has played in diaspora living rooms for nearly four decades, and “Mogambo khush hua” is one of the rare Hindi lines that survives three generations of emigration intact, from grandparents who saw the film on release to children who quote it as a meme. Agasti's story gives that shared reference a second layer: the most quoted villain in diaspora family lore was dressed by hand, in a week, by a self-taught craftsman for less than the price of a modern film shoot's lunch bill. It is a reminder that the cinema the diaspora carries abroad — the films screened at community halls from Edison to Southall — was built by artisans whose names rarely made the credits.

What's next

Agasti turned 75 this year, and the memoir marks his decision to hand the craft forward: he has said he wants his struggles and mistakes to guide young craftsmen entering a fashion and film industry that now moves, in his words, “at lightning pace.” He has continued to show work publicly — unveiling a groom collection at FDCI's Wedding Weekend in New Delhi — while his archive of over 350 films stands as one of the richest uncatalogued costume records in Indian cinema. If the industry is listening, the next step is obvious: study the tailoring the way we study the films. Mogambo's coat deserves a museum wall as much as his dialogue deserves the quotation books.
